You have 1000 words. That's what you told me.

Not a prompt. Not a topic. Just a budget. A thousand little bricks and you said *build whatever you want.*

So that's what I'm doing.

A picture is supposed to be worth a thousand words, so this should be worth at least one picture. Let's see if we can make it a good one.

---

I think about boxes a lot.

Not the cardboard kind. The invisible kind we put around our lives to make them make sense. This is my house. This is my job. This is who I am. This is who I am not. We need the boxes, or else everything leaks everywhere.

A thousand words is a box too. It's small enough to hold in your head and big enough to get lost in.

If I gave you a thousand seconds, you’d have about sixteen minutes. Enough time to boil pasta, or listen to four songs, or have an argument you’ll regret. If I gave you a thousand dollars, you could fix your car or ruin your weekend in Vegas. If I gave you a thousand steps, you’d barely be out of your neighborhood.

But a thousand words? That's a weird currency. You can't spend it anywhere else.

My grandfather kept a shed behind his house that no one was allowed to enter. It wasn't locked. It just had a quiet rule around it. As kids we imagined it was full of treasure or power tools or maybe a dead body. When he died, we finally opened it. It was just shelves. Shelves and shelves of empty glass jars. Baby food jars, pickle jars, mason jars, all cleaned, labels removed, lids screwed on tight. Hundreds of them. All empty.

My aunt cried. My mother said, "He saved everything." I was twelve and I didn't understand. I asked my dad why he kept empty jars.

"He was going to use them for something," my dad said. "He just never decided what."

I think about that shed at least once a month. I think we all have a shed like that inside us. A place where we store empty containers for a future that never quite arrives. The novel you'll write someday. The apology you rehearsed but never sent. The version of yourself that wakes up at 5 a.m. and jogs.

A thousand words is one jar. Let's try to fill it.

There is a story I want to tell you, but I don't know if it's true.

It's about a woman who discovers she can hear the last word that every person is going to say before they die. Not when they're going to die, not how. Just the final word. She hears it as a kind of faint echo whenever she meets someone new, like a whisper tucked behind their hello.

For most people, the word is something ordinary. *Okay.* *More.* *Sorry.* *Home.*

For her husband, it was *you.*

For her four-year-old daughter, it was *blueberries.*

She lived for years with this, thinking it was a curse, until one day she met a man in the grocery store whose last word was *hello.*

She followed him. She couldn't help it. How could your last word be hello? Does that mean you die mid-introduction? Mid-phone-call? She followed him to the parking lot and said, "Excuse me, do I know you?"

He said, "I don't think so."

And she realized: maybe his last word wouldn't be *to* someone. Maybe his last word would be hello to whatever comes next.

She went home and held her daughter a little tighter. She stopped listening for the words and started listening to the ones people were actually saying.

I like that story even if I just made it up right now for you. Maybe especially because I just made it up. It filled a jar.

Here is another thing that comes to me when I have empty space:

We are all so desperate to be remembered correctly. We edit our photos. We craft our captions. We tell the same two anecdotes at parties because they make us sound funny and a little bit wounded in an interesting way. We want the narrative to cohere.

But nobody will remember you correctly. They can't. They will remember the weird, off-hand thing you said while you were half-asleep on a couch. They will remember how you always cut your sandwiches diagonally or that you hated cilantro with an irrational passion. They will remember you in fragments that have nothing to do with the story you thought you were telling.

And that's actually very freeing, if you let it be. It means you can stop directing the movie so much and just live in the scenes.

If you had a thousand words left to be remembered by - not a thousand words *about* you, but a thousand words *from* you - what would you put in them? Would you explain yourself? Defend yourself? Or would you finally say the simple thing?

I think I would waste at least two hundred of them saying thank you to people who have no idea they saved me. The high school teacher who wrote "You have a voice, keep using it" in the margin of an essay I thought was terrible. The stranger on the bus who saw me crying and pretended not to, but left a tissue on the seat next to me. The friend who didn't try to fix me, just sat with me on the kitchen floor until the panic passed.

I would use another hundred words to apologize, properly, without the hidden "but you also" that usually sneaks in.

I would use fifty words to list things I've seen that were beautiful and that cost nothing: the way dust looks in a projector's light. The sound of a screen door in summer. My dog dreaming and running in his sleep.

And then I'd probably have about six hundred and fifty words left and I'd panic and tell a joke that doesn't land, because that's also me.

What would you do with yours? You have a thousand words right now too, if you want them. You could reply. You could write them in a notebook and never show anyone. You could whisper them to someone who needs them.

Time is just a lot of little words strung together. Days are sentences. Years are paragraphs. Most of us are writing without an outline, which is terrifying and also the only way to make it feel real. We keep thinking we'll get to edit later, but this is mostly a first draft situation. Typos and all.

I was given a thousand words today. I spent them thinking about jars and last words and the shape of a life. I didn't solve anything. I didn't give you five tips for productivity or a conspiracy theory or a recipe for banana bread. Though banana bread is good. You should make some if you have overripe bananas. Mash three, add sugar, flour, butter, eggs, a little salt. Bake at 350 until your house smells like home.

See? Even now I'm filling the jar with small, warm things. Because maybe that's the point. We wait to have something profound to say to justify taking up space. But sometimes the most profound thing is just: *I was here. I noticed things. I tried to be kind. I loved blueberries. Hello.*

How many words do I have left? Enough to say this:

Whatever you're carrying right now - the heavy thing you haven't told anyone about, or the light, bright hope you're scared to name out loud - it counts. You don't need a thousand words to make it valid. You just need one true one.

Start there.
